title: NAFAS
text:
Aim
The target audience was Malaysian parents of children with asthma, in line with SDG 3: Good Health and Well-Being. The app has four parts:

Real-time monitor: current AQI, temperature, humidity and pollutant levels (PM2.5, PM10, O₃) for 40 stations, pulled from the WAQI API, with child-specific guidance.
Learn: a guide to childhood asthma, plus charts comparing yearly state-level AQI with national childhood asthma cases (IHME data, stored in SQLite).
Travel: pick an origin, destination and date, and get a forecast AQI and a 5-day outlook for the destination city. Models were pickled and stored here.
Assess: combines live AQI and PM2.5 with the child’s asthma severity to give an outdoor-activity recommendation.

title: NAFAS
text:
Data and modelling
Historical air quality data was the hardest part. At the time, I couldn’t find a single open source of historical AQI for Malaysia, and the live APIs only returned current readings, so I aggregated daily readings from the api-malaysia repository into a per-city dataset. I then fitted one Prophet time-series model per city (that were available), saved each as a pickle file, and loaded them in the app to forecast AQI for the chosen date.
The forecasts are a proof of concept. Because of time constraints, the models were not rigorously validated, and accuracy drops the further the chosen date is from the training data.
More than anything, this project was my first exposure to how Malaysia could improve on their organization of open-source data.

title: Was it worth the flip?
text:
Being very late to the party when it comes to card games, I have since found a fascination towards them. Specifically, a card game called Flip 7, where the goal of the game is to flip 7 distinct cards, without busting.
As simple as it sounds, it’s a probabilistic game. Some would say luck, which it is still, since it’s kinda hard to keep track of how many cards are left. That’s what makes it interesting: the odds change with every card that leaves the deck.

Being very late to the party when it comes to card games, I have since found a fascination towards them. Specifically, a card game called Flip 7, where the goal of the game is to flip 7 distinct cards, without busting.
As simple as it sounds, it’s a probabilistic game. Some would say luck, which it is still, since it’s kinda hard to keep track of how many cards are left. That’s what makes it interesting: the odds change with every card that leaves the deck.

title: Was it worth the flip?
text:
How the game works
Everyone flips cards from a shared deck, one at a time. The deck has number cards from 0 to 12, and there are as many copies of each number as its value (one 1, two 2s, and so on). Flip a number you already hold and you bust, scoring nothing that round. Stop before that happens and you bank the total of your hand. Flip seven different numbers and you earn a bonus, and the first player to 200 points wins. There are also action cards, such as Freeze, Flip Three and Second Chance.

title: Was it worth the flip?
text:
This project
To keep things simple, I only use the number cards 0 to 12 (79 cards) and leave out the bonus cards. The question I want to answer is: when to stop flipping?
Please find the write-up to this here

title: Was it worth the flip?
text:
Code

Create the deck

library(tidyverse)

# create card deck containing 0-5 numbers (for 0 and 1 card, theres 1 each)

deck <- c(0, 1, rep(2,2), rep(3,3), rep(4,4), rep(5,5),
          rep(6,6), rep(7,7), rep(8,8), rep(9,9),
          rep(10,10), rep(11,11), rep(12,12))

[76] 12 12 12 12

# should be 79
length(deck)

[1] 79




Simulate the game

play_round <- function(stop_at){
  
  # randomly shuffle deck
  d <- sample(deck)
  
  # initializing hand and total
  hand <- c()
  total <- 0
  
  for (card in d){
    # the total reaches the limit, then stop
    if (total >= stop_at) return(total)
    
    # if pull the same card, then bust
    if (card %in% hand) return(0)
    hand <- c(hand, card)
    total <- total + card
    
    # whoever gets 7 distinct card gets an additional 15 points
    if (length(hand)==7) return(total +15)
  }
  total
  

  }



Test simulation

# test 
replicate(10, play_round(20))

set.seed(47)
n <- 5000

results <- map_dfr(1:63, function(s) {
  scores <- replicate(n, play_round(s))
  tibble(stop_at = s,
         avg_points = mean(scores),
         se = sd(scores) / sqrt(n))
})

title: Exploratory attack on AudioSeal
text:
Discussion & Limitations
All attacks were tested on a single audio clip from LibriSpeech. Two black-box attacks (random-noise querying and particle swarm optimisation) and one white-box attack (gradient-based PGD) all evaded detection, but only PGD did so while keeping good audio quality (PESQ 3.71, versus about 1.8 to 1.9 for the black-box attacks).
Reversing PGD to forge the watermark worked even better: detection on unwatermarked audio rose from 1% to 100% with almost no audible change (PESQ 4.48). This was possible because AudioSeal’s detector weights are publicly downloadable, which gives an attacker full white-box access, even though the authors’ own paper warns the weights should be kept private.
These results come from one clip and assume white-box access for PGD, so they show what is possible, not how robust AudioSeal is in general. Developing strong black-box attacks remains the realistic open problem. Note also that PESQ is only a proxy for quality: the query and PSO attacks left audible background noise, so a human listener would likely notice the tampering, which undermines them as practical attacks.
